one_liner: A narrow-moat business worth owning, but it trades at 2.6x fair value. Interesting below about $76.

profile.what: Johnson & Johnson is a health-care company with two businesses: Innovative Medicine (prescription drugs for cancer, immunology and neuroscience) and MedTech (surgical, orthopaedic, heart and eye devices).
profile.money: Drugs are about two-thirds of revenue, with leading cancer drugs such as Darzalex and Carvykti; immunology drug Stelara has lost patent protection. MedTech sells devices to hospitals. Talc-related litigation remains a cost.
profile.valued: J&J is valued on P/E and dividend yield as a defensive health-care company. The multiple depends on new drugs offsetting the Stelara patent loss.

summary.sentence: A diversified health-care company replacing a lost blockbuster while managing litigation.
strengths: Very steady free cash flow of $17-21B a year.
Forward P/E about 25 versus trailing 42 shows earnings recovering.
risks: The share price has rallied hard; trailing P/E above 40.
GAAP earnings swing with one-offs (spin-off gain, litigation).
Patent cliffs on key immunology drugs.

meaning.what_it_does: A healthcare company focused on prescription drugs (oncology, immunology, neuroscience) and medical devices, after spinning off its consumer health business.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Patented medicines and surgical, orthopaedic and cardiovascular devices sold to hospitals and health systems.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: A deep pipeline and acquisitions to replace drugs that lose patent protection; devices benefit from surgeon relationships.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Patent cliffs without replacements, drug-price regulation, or large litigation settlements (talc).

moat.summary: Patents protect individual drugs only temporarily, so the moat depends on constantly refilling the pipeline.

industry.summary: Medicine advances steadily; each drug faces a patent cliff, so innovation is required but not a winner-take-all race.

management.summary: Disciplined capital allocation and a AAA-rated balance sheet, offset by long-running litigation.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow: $18.5B a year: free cash flow less stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 2–8% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 27%; cost of capital 9.3%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
